title: Generics: compile-time type safety, no explicit casts
shortTitle: What are generics and why do we need them?
keyPoints: Generics provide compile-time type safety, turning runtime ClassCastException into compile errors that are caught before the code runs.
Without generics, collections store Object and require explicit casting on retrieval, which can fail silently at runtime.
With generics, the compiler verifies that only the declared type is added and removes the need for explicit casts.
Generics were introduced in Java 5 and use type erasure for backward compatibility: type parameters are removed at compile time.
The diamond operator (<>) in Java 7 allows type inference on the right side: new ArrayList<>() instead of new ArrayList<String>().
Generics apply to classes, interfaces, methods, and constructors, not just collections.
Raw types (List instead of List<String>) should never be used in new code because they bypass type safety.

s1_definition.oneliner: Generics provide compile-time type safety by parameterising classes and methods with type parameters, eliminating explicit casts and converting runtime ClassCastException into compile errors.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Type parameter** – a placeholder like `<T>` or `<E>` that is replaced with a concrete type at usage: `List<String>`, `Map<String, BigDecimal>`
- **Compile-time checking** – the compiler rejects attempts to add the wrong type, catching errors before runtime
- **No explicit casts** – reading from a parameterised collection returns the declared type directly, not Object
- **Type erasure** – generics exist only at compile time; at runtime, `List<String>` becomes `List` for backward compatibility
- **Diamond operator** – Java 7 allows `new ArrayList<>()` where the compiler infers the type from the declaration
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, without generics, the filing drawer accepts anything: cheques, cash, loan forms, even a lunch box. When Rajesh reaches in expecting a cheque, he might grab a lunch box and crash (ClassCastException). With generics, the drawer is labelled "Cheques Only" and the filing clerk (compiler) rejects anything that is not a cheque at filing time, long before anyone gets hurt.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Without Generics (Raw Type)
  ============================
  List rawList = new ArrayList();
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ rawList.add("SAV2001")  -> OK         │
  │ rawList.add(42)         -> OK (!)     │
  │ rawList.add(new Date()) -> OK (!)     │
  │ String s = (String) rawList.get(1)    │
  │             -> ClassCastException!    │
  │ Bug found: RUNTIME (production)       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  With Generics
  ==============
  List<String> typedList = new ArrayList<>();
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ typedList.add("SAV2001") -> OK        │
  │ typedList.add(42)        -> COMPILE   │
  │                             ERROR!    │
  │ String s = typedList.get(0) -> OK     │
  │             (no cast needed)          │
  │ Bug found: COMPILE TIME (IDE)         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Generics are one of the most important features in Java for writing safe, maintainable code. By parameterising collections and classes with type parameters, the compiler catches type mismatches at compile time instead of letting them cause ClassCastException in production. This eliminates explicit casts, makes code self-documenting, and prevents an entire category of runtime errors.

The trade-off is type erasure: generic type information is removed at compile time for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. This means certain operations (new T(), instanceof List<String>, T.class) are not possible, which is covered in the type erasure question.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj mandated that every collection in the codebase be fully parameterised. Lists of account identifiers were declared as List<String>, maps of balances as Map<String, BigDecimal>. This meant that mixing account IDs with balance amounts was caught by the compiler, not by a production incident report.

Remember one sentence: generics turn runtime ClassCastException into compile errors by enforcing type constraints on collections and classes at compile time.
